title: An exquisite dulcet epithalame of most mollificative suadency for juveniles amatory whom the odoriferous flambeaus of the paranymphs have escorted to the quadrupedal proscenium of connubial communion.
html_source:
Wow – what a line, has taken me a day of research to even hypothesize what it might mean.

Dulcet – (Especially of sound) sweet and soothing (often used ironically)
Epithalame – from Epithalamium – a song in praise of bride and bridegroom, sung by a number of boys and girls at the door of the nuptial chamber
Mollificative – that makes soft or supple
Suadency – to persuade
Paranymphs – From Middle French, French paranymphe and its etymons post-classical Latin paranymphus male wedding attendant, best man and paranympha bridesmaid from ancient Greek παράνυμϕος (masculine noun) friend of the bridegroom, best man, in Byzantine Greek also (feminine noun) bridesmaid from παρα- + νύμϕη bride

So, it might mean (with Joyce you never know what all it could mean) — A most beautiful sweet & soothing song of soft persuasion sung by boys & girls outside the nuptial chamber as the Best man & Bridesmaids escort the young bride & bridegroom under the light of flaming torch (might symbolize Hymen – the Greek god of marriage) to the four footed theatrical stage (curtained bed in Nupital chamber) for them to consummate their marital union.
